title: Tz-D-K
hookLine: tzedek, tzedakah, tzaddik: giving is a form of justice

cards: A coin drops through the slot of a small metal box. On its side, painted in Hebrew letters, one word: tzedakah. Now a different room.
A judge sits at a bench, listening to two people who each say the other owes them. When the judge rules, the hope is for a ruling that is tzedek, right.
A coin box and a courtroom: one looks like kindness, the other like law. Hebrew doesn't split them that way. Both words grow from the same three letters.
Today's root asks whether giving is a favor, or something owed.

teach.b: Tz-D-K. Tzadi, dalet, kuf. Four ways in.
In Deuteronomy, judges are told, "Justice, justice shalt thou follow." The word is tzedek, said twice. Second, tzedakah.
In English it's often translated charity, which sounds like something extra, a kindness you may or may not choose. But tzedakah is built from the letters of justice.
In this way of thinking, giving to someone in need isn't generosity on top of fairness. It is fairness.

Leviticus makes it concrete: at harvest, the corner of the field and the gleanings that fall are left for the poor and the stranger. The farmer doesn't hand them out as a favor. They were never his to keep.

Proverbs says "righteousness delivereth from death," and some readers hear that line as being about tzedakah. Third, the tzaddik. You met tzadi earlier in this block, as the first letter of tzaddik, the righteous one.

teach.h: TZADDIK: A LIFE SHAPED BY TZEDEK.
teach.b: Now you can see why the name fits: a tzaddik is someone whose life is shaped by tzedek. Fourth, how to give.

teach.h: THE TOP LEVEL: HELP THEM STAND.
teach.b: Maimonides, in his laws of gifts to the poor, lays out levels of giving, and at the top he places helping someone stand on their own: a loan, a partnership, a job, so they won't need to ask again.
Justice, in that picture, isn't only a coin in a box. It's a corner of the field that keeps growing back.

how: Jewish law treats tzedakah, giving to those in need, as an obligation rather than an optional kindness; families may keep a tzedakah box at home, and Maimonides ranks levels of giving, with helping someone become self-supporting at the top.

o: the root of tzedek, justice, and tzedakah, giving
the root of tzelem, image, and tzalam, photographer
the root of tzitzit, the fringes on a garment

p: left for the poor and the stranger

s: tzedakah means the same as charity: a nice extra
it shares a root with tzedek, justice: giving is part of fairness.
Maimonides places helping someone stand on their own at the top of his levels of giving

in Leviticus, the farmer chooses whether to leave the corner of his field
it's the law: the corner and the gleanings are left for the poor and the stranger.

games.q: you want to help a neighbor who has fallen on hard times. by Maimonides' levels, what's the highest form?
o: a large gift, given in public.
a loan, a partnership or a job that helps them stand on their own.
a small gift, given every week.
games.why: helping them stand on their own. Maimonides puts it at the top, so they won't need to ask again.

practice: Bring to mind something you have, money, time, a skill, a contact, a meal, and picture one corner of it as if it had been set aside all along for someone else.
Ask quietly whose this corner is, a cause, a neighbor, someone you know who is struggling, and try holding it as owed rather than offered. If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Tz-D-K. Tzadi, dalet, kuf: the root of tzedek, justice; tzedakah, giving; and tzaddik, the righteous one. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: giving to those in need, from the root of tzedek, justice.

carryVoice: Your line: giving is justice. The corner was set aside all along. Back tomorrow, same hill.

sources.ref: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7
